title: Deep Object Merge

title: Group Items by Key
description: Implement a generic function that groups an array of objects into a dictionary keyed by a given property, preserving each group's original relative order.
objective: Group the items below by their `category` value and return the resulting record.
hints: Iterate through the array and use the value at `item[key]` as the key for your result object.
Use `String(item[key])` to safely convert the key's value into a string usable as an object key.
The first time you see a new key value, initialize an empty array for it before pushing the current item.
explanation: The cleanest approach uses `Array.prototype.reduce` to build a `Record<string, T[]>` accumulator: for each item, compute `const groupKey = String(item[key])`, then do `acc[groupKey] = acc[groupKey] ?? []; acc[groupKey].push(item);` before returning `acc`. Typing the parameter as `keyof T` (rather than `string`) gives you compile-time safety — you can't accidentally group by a property that doesn't exist on `T`. Since object property insertion order is preserved for string keys in JavaScript, the resulting groups appear in the order their first member was encountered.

title: Deep Clone a Nested Value
description: Implement a function that returns a fully independent deep copy of a value made up of plain objects, arrays, numbers, strings, booleans, and null.
objective: Deep-clone the nested `original` value below and return the copy.
hints: If `value` is `null` or not an object (a primitive), just return it directly — primitives are already copied by value.
If `Array.isArray(value)` is true, return a new array built by recursively cloning each element.
Otherwise it's a plain object: build a new object and recursively clone each of its own property values.
explanation: Deep cloning requires recursion: the base case returns primitives (and `null`) as-is since they're copied by value already. For arrays, `value.map(item => deepClone(item))` recursively clones each element into a brand-new array. For objects, iterate `Object.keys(value)` and assign each recursively-cloned value onto a fresh object, so nested references never alias the original. This differs from `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(value))`, which silently drops `undefined`/functions and can't handle special types — a manual recursive clone is more explicit and extensible.

title: Flatten a Nested Array to a Depth
description: Implement a function that flattens a nested array up to a given depth, without using the built-in Array.prototype.flat.
objective: Flatten the `nested` array below to a depth of 2 and return the result.
hints: If `depth <= 0`, just return a shallow copy of the array as-is.
Otherwise, use `reduce`: for each element, if `Array.isArray(element)` is true, recursively flatten it with `depth - 1` and concat the result; otherwise concat the element itself.
Remember that `Array.prototype.concat` already merges one level of array automatically, so concatenating a recursively-flattened sub-array won't leave extra nesting.
explanation: The idiomatic manual implementation mirrors the native `.flat()` polyfill: `return depth > 0 ? arr.reduce((acc, val) => acc.concat(Array.isArray(val) ? flattenArray(val, depth - 1) : val), []) : arr.slice();`. Each recursive call reduces `depth` by one only when descending into a nested array, so elements deeper than `depth` levels remain nested in the output. Using `concat` (rather than `push`) keeps the code concise since it naturally spreads array arguments by one level.

title: Pluck Specific Object Keys
description: Implement a generic function that returns a new object containing only the specified keys, copied from the input object, in the order given.
objective: Pluck the `name` and `age` keys from the `user` object below and return the result.
hints: Start with an empty object and cast it to `Pick<T, K>` so TypeScript knows what shape you're building toward.
Loop over the `keys` array (not `Object.keys(obj)`) so the output only contains — and follows the order of — the requested keys.
For each key `k` in `keys`, copy `obj[k]` onto your result object under the same key.
explanation: `Pick<T, K>` is a built-in TypeScript utility type that produces a new object type containing only the properties named in `K`. The runtime implementation just needs to iterate the requested `keys` array and copy each property across: `const result = {} as Pick<T, K>; for (const k of keys) { result[k] = obj[k]; } return result;`. Constraining `K extends keyof T` means the compiler rejects any key that doesn't actually exist on `T`, catching typos at compile time rather than producing `undefined` values at runtime.

title: Merge Two Typed Objects
description: Implement a function that returns a new object combining two objects, where the second object's values take priority on key collisions (shallow merge only).
objective: Merge `target` and `source` below (source wins on conflicts) and return the result.
hints: The object spread operator lets you merge two objects in a single expression.
Spread `target` first and `source` second — properties spread later always overwrite properties spread earlier with the same key.
The result naturally has the type `T & U` (an intersection), since it has every property from both `T` and `U`.
explanation: The simplest correct implementation is `return { ...target, ...source };`. Object spread copies own enumerable properties left-to-right, so later spreads (`source`) overwrite earlier ones (`target`) when keys collide, matching the desired override behavior. The return type `T & U` is TypeScript's intersection type — it tells consumers the result is guaranteed to have every property from both input types, which is exactly what the merged object provides.

title: Remove Duplicate Objects by Key
description: Implement a function that returns a new array with duplicate objects removed, where two objects are considered duplicates if they share the same value for a given key. Keep only the first occurrence.
objective: Remove duplicate items from the array below by their `id` and return the result.
hints: Create a `Set` before iterating to keep track of key values you've already seen.
Use `Array.prototype.filter` and, for each item, check whether `seen.has(item[key])` — if it's already there, filter the item out.
If the value hasn't been seen yet, add it to the `Set` (e.g. with `seen.add(item[key])`) and keep the item — this preserves first occurrences.
explanation: A `Set` gives O(1) average lookup, so the whole operation runs in O(n) time: `const seen = new Set(); return items.filter(item => { const val = item[key]; if (seen.has(val)) return false; seen.add(val); return true; });`. Because `filter` processes items in original order and the `Set` check happens before insertion, the first item for each distinct key value is always the one retained, and everything after it with the same key value is dropped.

title: Sort by Multiple Keys
description: Implement a function that returns a new, ascending-sorted array, using each key in order as a tiebreaker for the previous one, without mutating the input array.
objective: Sort the `people` array below by `name`, then `age`, and return the result.
hints: Copy the array first (e.g. `[...items]`) before calling `.sort()`, since `.sort()` mutates in place.
Write a comparator that loops through `keys`; for each key, compare `a[key]` and `b[key]` and return a non-zero result as soon as one is found.
`a[key] < b[key] ? -1 : a[key] > b[key] ? 1 : 0` works for comparing both strings and numbers ascending; only move to the next key when this evaluates to `0`.
explanation: Copying the array with `[...items]` avoids the classic bug of `.sort()` silently mutating the caller's data. The comparator walks `keys` in priority order: `for (const key of keys) { if (a[key] < b[key]) return -1; if (a[key] > b[key]) return 1; } return 0;`. Returning as soon as a key produces a difference means later keys only get consulted when all earlier keys are equal — exactly the 'tiebreaker' behavior multi-key sorting needs.

title: Curry a Two-Argument Function
description: Implement a function that transforms a two-argument function into a curried version, callable as curried(a)(b).
objective: Curry the `add` function below, call it as `curriedAdd(3)(4)`, and return the result.
hints: `curry2` should return a function that accepts just the first argument, `a`.
That returned function should itself return another function — this one accepting `b`.
Inside the innermost function, call the original `fn(a, b)`, using closure to access the `a` captured by the outer function.
explanation: Currying relies on closures: `return (a: A) => (b: B) => fn(a, b);`. The outer arrow function captures `a` in its closure and returns a new function that, once called with `b`, has access to both `a` and `b` and can finally invoke the original two-argument `fn`. This pattern is the building block behind partial application — calling `curry2(add)(3)` alone yields a reusable 'add 3 to something' function without immediately needing the second argument.

title: Memoize a Numeric Function
description: Implement a function that returns a memoized version of a single-argument numeric function — calling it twice with the same argument should only invoke the underlying function once.
objective: Memoize `square` below, call it as shown, and return the results plus the final `callCount`.
hints: Declare a `Map<number, number>` outside (in the closure of) the function you return, so it persists across calls.
Before calling `fn`, check `cache.has(arg)` — if true, return `cache.get(arg)` immediately instead of recomputing.
If it's a cache miss, compute `fn(arg)`, store it with `cache.set(arg, result)`, then return it — `fn` (and therefore `callCount`) only runs on genuine misses.
explanation: The returned function closes over a `Map` used as a cache: `const cache = new Map<number, number>(); return ((arg: number) => { if (cache.has(arg)) return cache.get(arg)!; const result = fn(arg); cache.set(arg, result); return result; }) as T;`. Because the cache lives in the closure and persists between calls, repeated calls with an already-seen argument skip `fn` entirely — which is why, in the test, `callCount` only reaches 2 (one for `4`, one for `5`) despite `memoizedSquare` being called five times.

title: Safely Parse JSON with a Fallback
description: Implement a function that attempts to JSON.parse a string and returns the parsed result on success, or a provided fallback value if parsing throws.
objective: Safely parse the valid and invalid JSON strings below and return both results as a pair.
hints: Wrap the `JSON.parse(jsonString)` call in a `try { ... } catch { ... }` block.
On success, return the parsed value directly from within the `try` block.
In the `catch` block, ignore the error and simply return the `fallback` argument that was passed in.
explanation: `JSON.parse` throws a `SyntaxError` on malformed input rather than returning `null` or `undefined`, so a `try/catch` is required to handle it gracefully: `try { return JSON.parse(jsonString) as T; } catch { return fallback; }`. Accepting `fallback: T` (rather than hardcoding a default) keeps the function generic and type-safe — callers get back exactly the type they expect whether parsing succeeds or fails, with no `any` leaking out.

title: Filter an Object's Entries
description: Keep only the object entries whose value passes a condition.
objective: Return the `inventory` object below with only the entries whose count is greater than zero. Expected: {"apples":4,"cherries":12}.
hints: Object.entries(obj) turns an object into an array of [key, value] pairs.
Filter that array, then rebuild an object with Object.fromEntries(pairs).
The count for "bananas" and "dates" is 0, so those two entries should be dropped.
starterCode:
const inventory = { apples: 4, bananas: 0, cherries: 12, dates: 0 };
// TODO: return only the entries with a count greater than zero, as an object
explanation: `Object.entries(obj)` gives you an array of `[key, value]` pairs you can `.filter()` like any other array — here, keeping only pairs where `count > 0`. `Object.fromEntries(pairs)` then rebuilds a plain object from that filtered array. This entries-filter-fromEntries round trip is the standard way to transform an object by its values without manually reassigning keys one at a time.

title: Deep Equality Check
description: Implement a function that recursively compares two values for structural equality, not just reference equality.
objective: Compare `left` against `right` and against `other` below, and return the three comparison results.
hints: If `a === b`, they're equal immediately — this also covers matching primitives.
If either isn't a non-null object, or one is an array and the other isn't, they can't be equal.
Compare `Object.keys(a).length` to `Object.keys(b).length` first — if the key counts differ they can't be equal — then recursively call your function on each matching key's values.
explanation: The recursive walk is: `if (a === b) return true; if (typeof a !== "object" || typeof b !== "object" || a === null || b === null) return false; if (Array.isArray(a) !== Array.isArray(b)) return false; const aKeys = Object.keys(a); const bKeys = Object.keys(b); if (aKeys.length !== bKeys.length) return false; return aKeys.every(key => deepEqual(a[key], b[key]));`. The key-count check before recursing is what catches the third case — comparing `left` to `{...left, extra: 1}` — since a naive implementation that only checks whether every key of `a` matches in `b` would miss that `b` has an *extra* key `a` doesn't. The `null` and array values in the fixture force the `typeof null === "object"` and `Array.isArray` guards to actually matter.

title: Safely Read a Nested Path
description: Implement a function that reads a dot/bracket-notated path out of a nested object, returning a fallback if any step along the path is missing.
objective: Read the four paths below out of `data` (with the given fallbacks) and return the results.
hints: Turn the path string into a list of keys, e.g. "user.tags[0]" should become ["user", "tags", "0"] — replacing "[0]" with ".0" before splitting on "." handles both dot and bracket notation with one rule.
Walk the keys one at a time, moving `current` deeper into the object; if `current` isn't an object at any step, the path doesn't exist — return the fallback right away.
Only fall back to the default when the final value is `undefined` — don't use `value || fallback`, since a legitimately falsy value like 0 would incorrectly trigger the fallback too.
explanation: `path.replace(/\[(\d+)\]/g, ".$1").split(".").filter(Boolean)` normalizes both `"a.b"` and `"a[0]"` style segments into one flat list of keys. Walking that list, `current = current[key]` steps one level deeper each time, bailing out to the fallback the moment `current` stops being an object (which is what happens for the missing `"age"` path). The last line, `return current === undefined ? fallback : current;`, is the part that makes `getIn(data, "count", -1)` correctly return `0` instead of `-1` — a naive `current || fallback` would treat the legitimate value `0` as falsy and wrongly fall back.

title: LRU Cache
description: Implement a fixed-capacity cache that evicts its least recently used entry once it's full, where both reads and writes count as "using" an entry.
objective: Complete the `get`/`set` methods below so the scripted sequence of calls produces the expected eviction, then return a summary of what happened.
hints: A `Map` remembers insertion order, and deleting then re-setting a key moves it to the end — that's exactly "most recently used" ordering for free.
On `get`: if the key isn't present, return `undefined`; otherwise delete and re-set it (to move it to the end) before returning its value.

On `set`: if the cache is at capacity and the key is new, evict the first key the Map's iterator yields (`this.map.keys().next().value`) — that's always the least recently used one — before inserting.
explanation: `get` is `if (!this.map.has(key)) return undefined; const value = this.map.get(key)!; this.map.delete(key); this.map.set(key, value); return value;` — the delete-then-set is what moves a *read* key to the most-recently-used end. `set` mirrors that: if the key already exists, delete it first (so the re-insert below moves it to the end); otherwise, if the map is already at capacity, delete `this.map.keys().next().value` — the oldest surviving key — before inserting the new one. Tracing the script: after `set("a",1)` and `set("b",2)` the map is `[a,b]`; `get("a")` reorders it to `[b,a]` (so `hitA` is `1`); `set("c",3)` is over capacity with `"b"` now oldest, evicting it to leave `[a,c]`; `get("b")` is therefore a miss (`missB` is `null`).

title: Diff Two Objects
description: Implement a function that compares two flat objects and reports which keys were added, removed, or changed between them.
objective: Diff `before` against `after` below and return the added/removed/changed key lists.
hints: A key is "added" if it exists in `after` but not in `before` — check with the `in` operator, e.g. `!(key in before)`.
A key is "removed" if it exists in `before` but not in `after` — the same check, the other direction.
A key present in both is "changed" only if its values differ (`before[key] !== after[key]`); if they're equal, it's neither added, removed, nor changed.
explanation: Two separate passes keep the logic simple: `for (const key of Object.keys(after)) if (!(key in before)) added.push(key);` finds new keys, then `for (const key of Object.keys(before)) { if (!(key in after)) removed.push(key); else if (before[key] !== after[key]) changed.push(key); }` finds removals and value changes in one pass over `before`'s keys. Here `a` only exists in `before` (removed), `d` only exists in `after` (added), `b` is present in both with the same value (ignored), and `c` is present in both but its value changed from `3` to `30` (changed).
